sources: Duke University Pratt School of Engineering news (2022), Glassfrogs Hide Red Blood Cells in Their Liver to Become Transparent (Taboada, Delia, Yao et al., Science, Dec 2022): northern glassfrog no more than a few centimeters; rests by day hanging upside down under leaves; while asleep removes nearly 90 percent of circulating red blood cells into a mirror-coated liver; avoids a huge blood clot; cells flow back when active; https://pratt.duke.edu/news/glassfrogs-hide-red-blood-cells-their-liver-become-transparent/

Sci.News, Study: Glassfrogs Hide Red Blood Cells in Their Liver to Achieve Transparency (reporting the Science paper): resting glassfrogs increase transparency two- to threefold; liver contains reflective guanine crystals; could inform biomedical research on clotting; https://www.sci.news/biology/glassfrog-transparency-11520.html

National Geographic magazine, These see-through frogs are full of surprises: male sun glass frog's heart beats visibly through its chest; a female's eggs visible through her stomach; some species smaller than a paper clip; 156 known species mainly in the northern Andes and Central America; males of at least 24 species care for eggs, sitting on them to keep them hydrated; the father sucks water up into his urinary bladder through a highly vascularized region of the belly; tadpoles fall into the stream below; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/these-see-through-frogs-are-full-of-surprises-feature

beats.say: This frog is see-through. You can watch its heart beat.
The glass frog. Some are smaller than a paper clip.
Its belly is a window. Heart, guts, all of it.
A mother's eggs even show right through her stomach.
By day, it sleeps upside down, under a leaf.
And while it sleeps, it hides almost ninety percent of its red blood.
It packs the red blood cells into its liver.
The liver is coated in tiny mirror crystals, so the red stays hidden.
That makes it two to three times more see-through.
And somehow, all that packed blood never clots.
When it wakes up, the blood flows back out into its body.
Scientists are studying it to learn about blood clots.
And there are over a hundred and fifty kinds, hiding in the Andes and Central America.
Its eggs sit on a leaf over a stream. The tadpoles drop into the water.
In some species, the dad guards the eggs.
Here's the weird part. He soaks water up into his bladder, through his belly.
Then he sits on the eggs, to keep them wet.
Would you hold one?
A belly like a window, and a dad who's a walking water balloon.
Follow me. Next, a bird that flies underwater.
